summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys affirmative action in the United States, covering arguments for workplace diversity and college admissions, the effects of Texas's top 10% rule and class-rank policies, Richard Sander's critique of racial preferences in law schools, and early federal executive orders by President Kennedy. It also notes the Italian American professors' 1976 request for affirmative action coverage, Thomas Sowell's critique, and AAUP and Gurin findings on the educational benefits of diversity.
one_line: Overview of U.S. affirmative action covering workplace diversity, college admissions policies, critiques by Richard Sander and Thomas Sowell, and Kennedy-era executive orders.
key_facts: The National Conference of State Legislatures held in Washington D.C. stated in a 2014 overview that many supporters of affirmative action argue its policies help open doors for historically excluded groups in workplace settings and higher education.

According to the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, many private sector employers have concluded that a diverse workforce makes a company "stronger, more profitable, and a better place to work."

To accommodate the ruling in Hopwood v. Texas banning any use of race in school admissions, the State of Texas passed a law guaranteeing entry to any state university to students who finished in the top 10% of their graduating class.

From 1996 to 1998, Texas had merit-based admission to its state universities, and minority enrollment dropped; the state's adoption of the "top 10 percent" rule returned minority enrollment to pre-1996 levels.
Richard H. Sander, a UCLA professor, published an article in the November 2004 issue of the Stanford Law Review questioning the effectiveness of racial preferences in law schools.

Sander's article found that half of all black law students rank near the bottom of their class after the first year of law school, and that black law students are more likely to drop out and to fail the bar exam.
Sander's article estimated that the production of new black lawyers in the United States would grow by eight percent if affirmative action programs at all law schools were ended.

Sander helped develop a socioeconomically-based affirmative action plan for the UCLA School of Law after the passage of Proposition 209 in 1996, which prohibited racial preferences by public universities in California.
Studies cited in the note showed the graduation rate of blacks at UCLA was 41%, compared to 73% for whites.
In 1976, a group of Italian American professors at City University of New York asked to be added as an affirmative action category for promotion and hiring, believing they were underrepresented.

Libertarian economist Thomas Sowell wrote in Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study that affirmative action policies encourage non-preferred groups to designate themselves as members of preferred groups.

In Executive Order 10925, President Kennedy stated that "discrimination because of race, creed, color, or national origin is contrary to the Constitutional principles and policies of the United States."

In June 1963, President Kennedy issued Executive Order 11114, which supplemented his 1961 executive order and declared it was the "policy of the United States to encourage by affirmative action the elimination of discrimination in employment."

A 2000 study by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) found that affirmative action promoted diversity within colleges and universities, with positive effects on students' educational outcomes and faculty teaching.

According to Professor Gurin of the University of Michigan, skills such as perspective-taking, acceptance of differences, and conflict resolution can potentially be developed in college when students are exposed to a heterogeneous group.
